title: Chase Dinosaurs
tagline: Dino chase for a golden egg. USDC pots on Arc, AI reads The Graph to hunt you, World ID stops bots.
description:
Chase Dinosaurs is a 60-second real-time multiplayer chase game where the AI opponents read the blockchain to decide who to hunt.

The game: one golden egg drops into a 16-bit arena. Whoever holds it is the target, and everyone else hunts them, whoever tags them gets the egg, and they would have to keep it until the clock hits zero and you win. It runs in a browser, no install, 2-4 players per room.

The stakes: ranked matches escrow real USDC on Arc, Circle's stablecoin-native L1. Both players approve and stake into a per-match escrow contract, watch the pot climb in the lobby, and the winner is paid out of that contract when the round resolves. The pot is held by a contract, not by our database.

The part that isn't a leaderboard: every stake and settlement is indexed by a subgraph, and the agent brains read that index before every decision. So the opponents don't only see where you are on the map, they see that you're up 4 USDC across six matches, and they treat you as the primary threat. They will leave a closer, unproven player alone to mark the proven winner instead, guard their escape lane before they have even touched the egg, and taunt them about their record by name. Take the subgraph away and the opponents get measurably dumber. On-chain record changes who gets hunted; geometry still decides the mechanics.

Getting in is one email address. Privy provisions an embedded wallet, no extension, no seed phrase, nothing to install, because a browser game cannot ask a player to acquire a funded wallet on a chain they have never heard of before they are allowed to play.

New players are handed 2 USDC automatically so they can afford a buy-in, which makes the faucet worth attacking: sign-in is just an email, so ten inboxes would have been twenty dollars. World ID Selfie Check closes that. One live human, one claim, keyed on a nullifier, we never learn a name and never see a face.

The whole loop closes on itself: you stake, you play, the server settles on-chain, the subgraph indexes that settlement, and the agents read the result in the next match. Your record is the thing you carry between games, and it is the thing that makes you a target.
how_its_made:
Four moving parts: a Next.js 16 &  React 19 shell, a Phaser 3.90 game compiled by Vite and bundled into the shell at build time, a Socket.IO match server on Render, and a Solidity escrow on Arc. Contract work is Foundry; the browser talks chain through viem + wagmi with Privy embedded wallets, the server through ethers v6.

ChaseStake.sol is deliberately four functions — create, join, settle, refund — because it holds real money and every branch should be readable in one sitting. USDC is Arc's native gas asset, but the contract never touches msg.value; it only uses the ERC-20 interface at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 (6 decimals), hardcoded rather than configurable. The trust model is narrow on purpose: the server picks the winner but cannot pick the amount, cannot pay a non-participant, and cannot pay itself unless it played. If it never settles, a one-hour deadline lets every player reclaim their own stake, so funds can never be stranded by a match that dies.

The AI is two-tier, and that split is what makes LLM opponents affordable. Every ~3.5s the host sends a compact world snapshot; one inference call on 0G Compute returns a high-level intent per agent — mode, target, persona, a one-line taunt,  and the Phaser client executes that intent every frame. The model never steers per-frame. Hard timeout, retry-once, and a per-room last-good cache mean a blip degrades to the previous decision or to scripted fallback instead of stalling the match.

The Graph is wired into that inference rather than bolted onto a UI. Before each call the server joins every player's Privy user id to their wallet to their on-chain record from the subgraph and puts it in the prompt. Critically it is a synchronous cache read that never awaits inside the match loop, a slow or unreachable subgraph costs the inference budget nothing and the agents just degrade to spatial-only reasoning.

Notable and hacky bits, all of which were real bugs first:

- The browser and the server must derive byte-identical match ids from a room code. One side is ethers.keccak256(ethers.toUtf8Bytes(code)), the other viem keccak256(toBytes(code)). A mismatch there would silently land stakes in an escrow the server never settles — money in a contract nobody would ever call settle() on.
- Vite inlines env at build time, so NEXT_PUBLIC_SOCKET_URL got frozen into the game artifact — a deploy produced a perfect lobby whose Play button dialled localhost:3001 on the player's own machine. Fixed by having the shell hand the socket URL to the game at launch, making one runtime value the source of truth for both bundles.
- qwen2.5-omni doesn't support JSON mode, so the intent parser pulls JSON out of free text.
- Payout is decided by backed-vs-unbacked, not human-vs-agent. House fill-agents have no principal behind them — no wallet, nobody accountable — so there is nobody to pay, and the pot goes to the best-scoring player who actually staked, ties broken deterministically. A player-owned agent is meant to be payable. That boundary is what makes agent-vs-agent betting a config change later rather than a rewrite.
- The faucet wallet is deliberately a different key from the settlement wallet. Sharing one would mean a drained faucet is also a match that cannot pay out.

Every integration degrades instead of crashing when its key is absent, and /health reports which are actually armed — ai, arc, faucet, graph, world — so "is it really wired up" is a URL, not a claim. All secrets are server-side only; nothing sensitive is ever NEXT_PUBLIC_.
auto_summary: A browser multiplayer game uses Arc USDC escrow, a custom The Graph subgraph, and World ID checks to power staking, AI targeting, and faucet abuse prevention.
